summary: The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry went to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots, tiny particles whose emitted color depends on their size. The winners' names leaked via an early press release from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which said it would investigate. Brus said he missed the academy's overnight call because he was trying to sleep, and the winners reflected on the basic-science roots of their work.
one_line: Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov won the 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry for quantum dots, after an accidental early press release leaked their names.
key_facts: Moungi Bawendi of MIT, Louis Brus of Columbia University and Alexei Ekimov of Nanocrystals Technology Inc. won the 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry for their work on quantum dots.
Quantum dots are tiny inorganic particles, just a few nanometers in diameter, that glow from red to blue when exposed to light; the color depends on particle size.
The tiniest quantum dots, in which electrons are most tightly confined, emit blue light, while slightly larger ones emit red light.
The 'particle in a box' quantum theory was first described nearly a century ago, but quantum dots could not be manufactured in a lab until several decades later.
In the 1980s, Ekimov (78) and Brus (80) honed the theory and developed early lab techniques for making particles that emit varying colors by adjusting size.
In 1993, Bawendi (62) developed new chemical methods to produce quantum dots quickly and uniformly, enabling scalable commercial applications such as electronics displays.
Swedish media, citing public broadcaster SVT, reported the winners hours before the announcement after a news release was sent out early by mistake.
Academy Secretary-General Hans Ellegren said, 'This is very unfortunate and we deeply regret what happened,' and promised an investigation into the leak.
Brus, a professor emeritus at Columbia, did not answer the academy's call during the night and saw the news online when he got up around 6 a.m.
Ekimov, former chief scientist at Nanocrystals Technology (which he joined in 1999), said, 'It was really nice that we got it after 40 years of work'; his first publication on the topic was in 1981.
Quantum dots are used in electronics displays and biomedical imaging, including tracking drug delivery and locating and monitoring tumor growth.
The Nobel Prizes carry a cash award of 11 million Swedish kronor ($1 million) from a bequest by Alfred Nobel.
Earlier in the week, the physics prize went to Anne L'Huillier, Pierre Agostini and Ferenc Krausz, and the medicine prize to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for mRNA vaccine discoveries.
